source.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
source.authors: Gouki Minegishi; Hiroki Furuta; Yusuke Iwasawa; Yutaka Matsuo

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAE features separate meanings in LLM activations, using a new semantic evaluation on polysemous words rather than the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports direct PS-Eval results on SAE features, including accuracy, F1, precision, recall, specificity, and comparisons across models, expansion ratios, layers, activation functions, and Transformer components. It also reports a cosine-distance comparison and controls. The logit-lens examples are qualitative; they are not included as rows because of the row limit.
record.test_reason: PS-Eval checks whether SAE features trained on LLM activations separate word meanings. It uses Word-in-Context pairs and compares against chance, random-SAE and dense-autoencoder baselines. This bears on V4, whether LLMs contain sparse features a dictionary can recover. The method differs from the original toy-model approach.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points: PS-Eval accuracy saturates around expand ratio 64; ReLU beats JumpReLU and TopK on F1 despite their better MSE-L0 trade-off; open SAEs on Pythia-70M and Gemma2-2B score lower. The authors also caveat that maximum-activation features may not track word meaning.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes PS-Eval on Word-in-Context examples and tests SAE feature meaning separation in GPT-2 small, Pythia 70M, and Gemma2-2B; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with expansion ratio, layer, activation function and its parameters, Transformer component, training-data domain, and base model.
record.problems: The authors note that maximum-activation features may not consistently correspond to target-word meanings and can reflect unrelated aspects. Much of the layer/component/domain evidence is presented only in figures without numerical values in the text. Open-model comparisons report lower scores and use different base-model/layer settings. A random-activation calculation shows specificity can be misleading when interpreted alone.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted qualitative logit-lens rows for the separate example words and other appendix results, including Ghost Grad comparisons; the 60-row limit was not reached, but these were lower priority than the reported numeric evaluation comparisons and key controls.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transitions or geometry.
All: no test of importance/capacity allocation.
All: no test of polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure.
Whether real models spread features across many neurons; neuron-level polysemanticity is not measured.
Completeness, stability across seeds and canonicality are not tested. The authors note max-activated features sometimes reflect unrelated aspects.
All: 1-D vs multi-dimensional features are not examined.

missing.what: Open-SAE accuracy, recall, precision and specificity. GPT-2: 0.66/0.94/0.60/0.38; Pythia: 0.51/0.72/0.51/0.32; Gemma: 0.52/0.74/0.51/0.30.
Remaining precision/recall values for TopK k=96/192 and STE jump=0.0001 (e.g., precision 0.52, 0.46).
Ghost Grad on vs off: PS-Eval metrics are better with Ghost Grad.

record.verdict_notes: Baselines matter here. Chance accuracy and precision are 0.5, and an SAE that always picks the same feature gets F1≈0.667, so F1 values near 0.62–0.67 are not evidence of recovery. Specificity and recall alone are inflatable. The study is essentially an SAE benchmark; its link to V4 is indirect, via max-activated-feature agreement with word sense.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometric arrangements.
Whether feature importance or competition for capacity determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study evaluates SAE recovery of meaning distinctions in selected LLM activations, not whether real models generally spread features across many neurons.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features are not systematically tested.
The study does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compare cosine distance between SAE features and LLM activations for different polysemous contexts
rows.measure: Cosine distance between representations of different meanings
rows.baseline: LLM activations: described as small cosine distance; value figure only
rows.value: SAE features: described as larger cosine distance; value figure only
rows.note: The paper states that SAE features are more distinct for the different meanings than the corresponding LLM activations.
rows.check: Figure only. The comparison sets cosine distance on sparse SAE codes against dense activations, which are not comparable spaces, so separation is partly expected by construction.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for V4 from this measure alone. The paper reports larger between-context cosine distances in SAE codes than in LLM activations; this does not independently establish semantic feature recovery.
source_check.locator_found: Section 6.1, Figure 3 and accompanying cosine-distance definitions
source_check.problem: Geometric separation in different representation spaces does not establish full recovery of semantic features.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 small, self-trained ReLU SAEs (L4/L6) and the open GPT-2 SAE
relationships.reason: Accuracy is 0.60–0.67 vs 0.5 chance (r01-r05, r07-r10). ReLU precision is 0.66–0.67 (r27, r28). The open SAE reaches accuracy 0.66 (r11). Sparse beats dense (r41). The effect is modest.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy was 0.60–0.67 against 0.5 chance and ReLU precision 0.66–0.67; the open SAE reached 0.66, and sparse beat dense. The effect is modest.
